## Gallbladder Cancer: Hepatic Resection for Biliary Tract Cancer

- Chapter 119A focuses on surgical management of gallbladder cancer.
- The chapter emphasizes hepatic resection, lymphadenectomy, and re-resection strategy.
- Key clinical scenarios include incidental diagnosis, advanced disease, port sites, and timing of re-resection.

## Scope of the Chapter

| Topic | Key Emphasis |
|---|---|
| Incidental gallbladder cancer | Intraoperative and postoperative recognition |
| Staging | Imaging, laparoscopy, and metastatic evaluation |
| Early stage disease | Simple cholecystectomy versus radical resection |
| Advanced disease | Extent of hepatic and adjacent organ resection |
| Lymph nodes | Hepatoduodenal lymphadenectomy and node count |
| Port sites | Risk of seeding and role of excision |
| Timing | Interval between cholecystectomy and re-resection |

## Epidemiology and Global Burden

- Gallbladder cancer is rare.
- It accounts for approximately 1.2 percent of all global cancers.
- Despite its rarity, it is the most common biliary tract malignancy.
- Gallbladder cancer represents 80 to 95 percent of all biliary cancer diagnoses.
- The disease carries a poor overall prognosis.

## Age and Sex Distribution

| Feature | Pattern |
|---|---|
| Typical age | Most often in the fifth decade of life |
| Sex predominance | Significant female predominance |
| Female to male ratio | Females affected 3 to 4 times as often as males |

## Risk Factors for Gallbladder Cancer

| Risk Factor | Clinical Relevance |
|---|---|
| Gallstone disease | Common chronic irritant and inflammatory stimulus |
| Gallbladder polyps | Associated with malignant potential |
| Primary sclerosing cholangitis | Chronic biliary inflammation |
| Salmonella typhi infection | Chronic infection in endemic areas |
| Helicobacter bilis infection | Chronic infection linked to inflammation |

## Shared Pathogenesis: Chronic Inflammation

- The precise pathogenesis of gallbladder cancer is unknown.
- Multiple risk factors share a common feature: chronic gallbladder inflammation.
- Inflammation is central to the proposed pathway from benign disease to malignancy.
- Endemic infections and chronic biliary irritation are important contextual factors.

## Prognosis at Presentation

| Prognostic Feature | Reported Estimate |
|---|---|
| Advanced stage at diagnosis | 70 to 90 percent of cancers |
| Curative opportunity at diagnosis | Limited because many cases are advanced |
| Median overall survival | Approximately 6 months |
| Five-year survival | Approximately 5 percent |

## Survival and the Role of Surgery

- Systemic therapies have limited effectiveness.
- Surgical resection remains the only potentially curative therapy.
- Survival after surgery is highly variable.
- Reported five-year survival after surgery ranges from 10 to 100 percent.
- Outcomes depend strongly on disease stage and extent of resection.

## Chapter Focus Areas

- Surgical management of gallbladder cancer.
- Management of port site recurrences.
- Timing of re-resection after incidental discovery following routine cholecystectomy.
- Technical aspects of hepatic margin resection and lymphadenectomy.

## Incidentally Diagnosed Gallbladder Cancer

- More than half of gallbladder cancers are incidentally diagnosed.
- Diagnosis often occurs during evaluation or treatment for presumed benign biliary disease.
- Malignancy may be recognized intraoperatively.
- More commonly, malignancy is identified postoperatively on histopathologic examination of the cholecystectomy specimen.

## Intraoperative Recognition During Cholecystectomy

| Step | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Suspicion intraoperatively | Perform frozen section biopsy |
| Purpose of frozen section | Confirm malignancy and assess extent |
| If cancer is confirmed | No further dissection is recommended |
| Operative plan | Abort the procedure |
| Next step | Proper staging workup and referral |

## Why Abort the Operation After Confirmation

- Current guidance recommends cessation of the procedure after intraoperative confirmation.
- The patient should receive a proper staging workup.
- Referral to an experienced hepatobiliary center is recommended.
- Residual disease after an incomplete initial operation is associated with very poor outcomes.
- A non-R0 resection at the initial operation, even if followed by R0 re-resection, is associated with outcomes equivalent to stage IV gallbladder cancer.

## Postoperative Incidental Diagnosis

- When cancer is found postoperatively, accurate pathologic stage confirmation is critical.
- Pathologic stage guides further treatment strategy.
- The specimen should be considered for re-evaluation by a hepatobiliary pathology specialist.
- Precise staging helps determine the need for radical re-resection.

## Staging Workup After Incidental Diagnosis

| Modality | Role |
|---|---|
| Dynamic contrast-enhanced CT | Abdomen and pelvis staging |
| Dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI | Alternative cross-sectional staging |
| Chest CT | Evaluate thoracic metastatic disease |
| Contrast use | With or without contrast depending on protocol |

## FDG-PET and Tumor Markers

| Test | Utility and Limitation |
|---|---|
| FDG-PET | Role is not well defined in incidental gallbladder cancer |
| FDG-PET impact | In one report of 63 patients, management changed in only 13 percent due to metastatic disease detection |
| CEA | Often obtained as a prognostic biomarker |
| CA 19-9 | Often obtained as a prognostic biomarker |
| Marker limitation | Limited evidence for increased sensitivity or specificity compared with high-resolution imaging |

## Staging Laparoscopy Rationale

- Metastatic disease is common in gallbladder cancer.
- Palliative surgical options are limited.
- Staging laparoscopy should be routinely performed.
- It identifies occult liver, peritoneal, and lymph node metastases.
- Reported data show laparotomy can be avoided in 56 percent of patients with unresectable gallbladder cancer when staging laparoscopy is used.

## Staging Laparoscopy Technique

| Step | Technical Detail |
|---|---|
| Abdominal entry | Veress needle, optical trocar, or open cutdown |
| Inspection | Visceral and parietal peritoneum in abdomen and pelvis |
| Omentum | Inspect for metastatic deposits |
| Suspicious lesions | Frozen section biopsy |
| Kocher maneuver | Reflect duodenum and pancreatic head medially |
| Nodal inspection | Assess retropancreatic and aortocaval nodes for N2 involvement |

- It distinguishes regional nodal stations from more distant nodal disease.

## Lymph Node Basins and Staging Roles

| Nodal Category or Site | Staging Meaning |
|---|---|
| Cystic nodes | Regional nodal basin |
| Pericholedochal nodes | Regional nodal basin |
| Retroportal nodes | Regional nodal basin |
| Superior mesenteric nodes | Important nodal station to recognize |
| Interaortocaval nodes | Distant nodal involvement concern |
| Posterosuperior pancreaticoduodenal nodes | Important for N2 assessment |
| N1 | Regional nodal disease |
| N2 | More advanced nodal disease |
| M1 | Distant metastatic disease |

## Early Stage Surgical Strategy

- Early stage disease includes T1 and T2 tumors.
- Management depends on depth of invasion.
- T1a tumors may be treated with simple cholecystectomy.
- T1b and T2 tumors generally require radical resection.
- Oncologic adequacy and margin status are central goals.

## T1a Gallbladder Cancer

| Feature | Implication |
|---|---|
| Depth of invasion | Tumor limited to lamina propria |
| Muscular layer | Not invaded |
| Recommended surgery | Simple cholecystectomy |
| Lymph node dissection | Not required |
| Approach | Minimally invasive or open |

## Laparoscopic Simple Cholecystectomy Outcomes

- Historically, open surgery was preferred for cancer operations.
- Reported data show favorable outcomes for selected early tumors.
- Patients with Tis and T1a gallbladder cancer undergoing laparoscopic simple cholecystectomy had 100 percent five-year survival.
- This supports favorable oncologic outcomes for laparoscopic resection in appropriately selected early stage disease.

## Technical Precautions During Simple Cholecystectomy

- Simple cholecystectomy for gallbladder cancer is similar to cholecystectomy for benign disease.
- Important differences must still be considered.
- Avoid iatrogenic gallbladder perforation.
- Bile spillage increases oncologic risk.
- Use a laparoscopic retrieval bag for specimen extraction.
- Retrieval bags are especially important if perforation occurs.

## Bile Spillage and Oncologic Risk

| Outcome | With Bile Spillage | Without Bile Spillage | Significance |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Port site metastases | 12.3 percent | 5.1 percent | Significantly higher |
| Local recurrences | 22 percent | 11.7 percent | Significantly higher |
| Peritoneal carcinomatosis | 12.1 percent | 15.1 percent | Nonsignificant trend |

## T1b and T2 Tumors Require Radical Resection

- In T1b and T2 tumors, simple cholecystectomy does not provide optimal oncologic benefit.
- Radical resection includes re-resection of the hepatic bed.
- The typical hepatic resection is partial hepatectomy of segments IVb and V.
- Radical resection also includes hepatoduodenal lymphadenectomy.
- The goal is improved locoregional control and survival.

## Survival by Surgical Approach in T1b and T2 Disease

| Surgical Approach | Five-Year Survival |
|---|---:|
| Simple cholecystectomy | 20 to 40 percent |
| Radical resection | 70 to 90 percent |

## Residual Disease and Nodal Risk by T Stage

| T Stage | Residual Hepatic Disease | Lymph Node Metastatic Disease | Locoregional Recurrence |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| T1b | Approximately 10 percent | 10 to 20 percent | 20 to 50 percent |
| T2 | Increases with T stage | Hepatoduodenal node disease in 30 to 60 percent | Higher than early T1a disease |

- Figure 119A.2 illustrates radical cholecystectomy.
- The operation includes cholecystectomy.
- It includes segment IVb and V partial hepatectomy.
- It includes hepatoduodenal lymphadenectomy.
- The figure demonstrates the combined hepatic and nodal resection concept.

## Advanced Stage T3 Tumors

| Feature | Surgical Implication |
|---|---|
| Definition | Tumor invades through visceral peritoneum |
| Extension | Direct extension into liver or adjacent organ |
| Treatment principle | Similar to T1b and T2 but often broader |
| Resection extent | May require extensive hepatic resection |
| Additional resection | May include bile duct resection or adjacent organ resection |
| Residual disease | 36 percent |
| Metastatic lymph node involvement | 46 percent |

## Advanced Stage T4 Tumors

| Feature | Clinical Meaning |
|---|---|
| Vascular involvement | Main portal vein or hepatic artery |
| Organ involvement | Two or more adjacent organs |
| Surgical challenge | Extensive vascular reconstruction may be needed |
| Perioperative risk | High morbidity |
| Upfront surgery | Generally unwarranted |

## Neoadjuvant Therapy in Advanced Disease

- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy and chemoradiation may be considered in advanced gallbladder cancer.
- Therapy can help assess tumor biology before major resection.
- It may help avoid unnecessary surgical resection in aggressive disease.
- It is especially relevant when major anatomic hepatectomy is contemplated.

## Hepatic Margin Resection Goals

- The extent of hepatic resection depends on tumor involvement.
- Resection may range from segment IVb and V partial hepatectomy to extended right hepatectomy.
- The goal is complete resection of residual parenchymal disease.
- Operative planning uses preoperative axial imaging and intraoperative ultrasonography.

## Imaging and Intraoperative Ultrasound Planning

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Preoperative axial imaging | Define tumor extent and operative plan |
| Intraoperative ultrasonography | Delineate vascular anatomy |
| Middle hepatic vein branches | Identify during transection |
| Parenchymal transection | Improve control and reduce blood loss |

## Segment IVb and V Partial Hepatectomy Overview

- Resection typically begins by lowering the hilar plate.
- This helps avoid injury to the left bile duct.
- Vessels within the umbilical fissure are exposed and controlled.
- Parenchymal dissection proceeds to the right of the falciform ligament.
- Dissection follows the principal scissura.

## Figure 119A.3: Lowering the Hilar Plate

- Figure 119A.3 shows the hilar plate.
- Lowering the hilar plate is an important initial step.
- It includes separating segment IV from the portal triad.
- This step improves safe access for segment IVb and V partial hepatectomy.

## Parenchymal Transection Steps

| Step | Technical Detail |
|---|---|
| Parenchymal split | To the right of the falciform ligament |
| Segment IVb inflow | Divided |
| Transection line | Oblique and parallel to the right scissura |
| Segment VIII | Preserved |
| Middle hepatic vein | Divided while traversing the principal plane |
| Segment V inflow | Located, secured, and divided |
| Test clamping | Confirms preservation of right anterior pedicle and segment VIII inflow |

## Completing the Segment IVb and V Resection

- The depth of transection includes the gallbladder fossa and cystic plate.
- Transection must remain above the right and left hilar structures.
- This avoids hilar injury.
- The right and left parenchymal transection planes are joined to complete the resection.

## Biliary and Vascular Safety Points

| Safety Issue | Technical Principle |
|---|---|
| Biliary radicles | Meticulous ligation is required |
| Anterior right portal pedicle | Lies close to the operative field |
| Segment IV pedicles | Must be protected or controlled |
| Biliary leak | Risk if radicles are not carefully managed |
| Pringle maneuver | Surgeon discretion |
| Postoperative drains | Surgeon discretion |
| Routine use evidence | Lacks strong supporting evidence |

## Major Hepatectomy and Future Liver Remnant

- Right portal vein or artery involvement may require right or extended right hepatectomy.
- Preoperative planning is paramount.
- Future liver remnant size should be determined.
- Adequate remnant volume reduces perioperative morbidity and mortality.
- Neoadjuvant therapy may be warranted before major anatomic hepatic resection.

## Concomitant Solid Organ Resection

- Concomitant solid organ resection may be necessary in selected patients.
- Colon or duodenum may be involved.
- Resection is reasonable in well-selected patients without disseminated disease.
- A period of neoadjuvant therapy is often useful to assess tumor biology.

## Lymphadenectomy Rationale

- T stage correlates with lymph node metastases.
- Portal or hepatoduodenal lymphadenectomy is routinely performed for T1b tumors and greater.
- Lymph node dissection includes N1 lymph nodes.
- N1 nodes are located in the gastrohepatic ligament, retroduodenal space, and hepatoduodenal ligament at the porta hepatis.

## Lymphadenectomy Technique: Initial Exposure

| Step | Technical Detail |
|---|---|
| Kocher maneuver | Mobilize the duodenum thoroughly |
| Peripancreatic tissue | Resect lymphatic tissue along the common bile duct near the pancreatic head |
| Highest peripancreatic node | Lies at the junction of the common bile duct and superior pancreas border |
| Nodal basin delineation | Separates N1 from N2 basins |
| Prognostic value | Associated with disease-specific and recurrence-free survival |

## Lymphadenectomy Technique: Porta Hepatis Dissection

| Step | Technical Detail |
|---|---|
| Peritoneal incision | Overlying porta hepatis structures |
| Structures identified | Common hepatic artery, common bile duct, main portal vein |
| Anterior clearance | Common bile duct and common hepatic duct cleared from liver base to pancreas head |
| Retraction | Cystic duct stump retracts common bile duct medially |
| Posterior dissection | Lymphatic tissue posterior and lateral to bile duct, anterior to portal vein |
| Completion view | Anterior portal vein visible and periarterial and periductal lymphatic tissue resected |

- Figure 119A.7 highlights the highest peripancreatic lymph node.
- This node lies between N1 and N2 lymph node basins.
- It is an important anatomic and prognostic landmark.

## Adequate Lymph Node Staging

| Guideline or Concept | Recommendation or Finding |
|---|---|
| AJCC eighth edition | Minimum of six lymph nodes for adequate nodal staging |
| Survival association | Adequate node count associated with improved outcomes |
| Node count comparison | Six nodes compared with one to five nodes shows survival benefit |
| N0 disease | Survival depends on total lymph node count |

## Evidence Supporting a Minimum Node Count

| Finding | Outcome |
|---|---|
| N0 patients with total lymph node count less than six | Median disease-specific survival approximately 24 months |
| N0 patients with total lymph node count greater than six | Median disease-specific survival approximately 41 months |
| Statistical significance | P less than .001 |
| Small lymph node yield | Associated with lower therapeutic index and higher hazard of death |

## N2 Basin Extension Is Not Recommended

- Extending lymphadenectomy to include the N2 basin is not recommended.
- N2 dissection increases perioperative morbidity.
- It does not provide a clear survival benefit.
- Intraoperative frozen assessment of suspicious aortocaval or retropancreatic nodes is appropriate.
- Malignant nodes in these basins are consistent with M1 disease and should stop further resection.

## Extrahepatic Biliary Tree Resection

| Principle | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Routine bile duct resection | Not recommended |
| Outcome effect | Not demonstrated to improve outcomes |
| Morbidity | Increases perioperative morbidity |
| Node yield | Routine common bile duct resection does not improve lymph node yield |

## Cystic Duct Margin and Biliary Reconstruction

| Situation | Management |
|---|---|
| Cystic duct stump margin | Confirm early with intraoperative frozen section |
| Positive margin | Bile duct resection may be necessary |
| Division level | Bile duct may be divided at the level of the duodenum |
| Goal | Negative surgical margins |
| Reconstruction | Roux-en-Y hepaticojejunostomy |

## Surgical Port Sites and Occult Seeding

- After laparoscopic cholecystectomy, occult tumor seeding at port sites is possible.
- Risk may be increased by bile or gallstone spillage.
- Port site recurrences are estimated at 17 to 19 percent.
- Historically, port site excision during re-resection was advocated.
- Recent evidence questions this routine practice.

## Evidence on Port Site Excision

| Study Feature | Finding |
|---|---|
| Multicenter analysis year | 2017 |
| Patients analyzed | 266 |
| Curative re-resection | 73 percent |
| Institutions | 10 |
| Follow-up span | 15 years |
| Port site excision among re-resected patients | 24 percent |
| Three-year overall survival | No difference between excision and no excision |
| Distant recurrence | 80 percent with excision versus 81 percent without excision |
| Statistical comparison | P equals 1.0 |

## Current Port Site Recommendation

- Port site recurrences are considered a harbinger of systemic disease.
- They are best addressed with nonlocalized therapy rather than local excision alone.
- Routine resection of port sites during reexploration is not advised.
- Avoiding routine port site excision reduces unnecessary morbidity without compromising survival.

## Timing of Re-resection

- Radical re-resection is recommended for selected patients with incidental gallbladder cancer.
- The optimal interval after initial cholecystectomy has been debated.
- A retrospective review divided patients into three intervals.
- Intervals were less than 4 weeks, 4 to 8 weeks, and greater than 8 weeks.
- The analysis adjusted for clinicopathologic and surgical factors.

## Survival by Re-resection Interval

| Interval From Cholecystectomy to Reoperation | Median Overall Survival |
|---|---:|
| Less than 4 weeks | 17.4 months |
| 4 to 8 weeks | 40.4 months |
| Greater than 8 weeks | 22.4 months |
| Statistical significance | P equals 0.03 |

## Practical Timing Strategy

- An intentional delay allows careful evaluation of residual disease.
- It allows assessment of metastatic spread.
- It provides time to observe underlying tumor biology.
- Excessively long delays may compromise outcomes.
- Reported median time from incidental diagnosis to radical re-resection is 52 days.
- This median falls within the favorable 4 to 8 week window.

## Nonincidental Gallbladder Cancer

| Feature | Nonincidental Disease |
|---|---|
| Detection | Diagnosed before or during planned cancer-directed evaluation |
| Proportion | Approximately half of patients |
| Survival | Worse median overall survival than incidental disease after adjustment |
| Likely explanation | Worse tumor biology and broader malignant symptoms |
| Workup | Similar to incidental disease |
| Treatment tendency | Neoadjuvant therapy often considered before definitive resection |

## Obstructive Jaundice as a Risk Marker

- Obstructive jaundice suggests advanced disease.
- It often reflects invasion of the extrahepatic biliary tree.
- Historically, jaundice as an initial symptom precluded surgical resection.
- Modern data suggest jaundice is associated with worse survival but may not be an independent poor-outcome predictor after adjustment.

## Jaundice Outcomes in Historical Cohorts

| Cohort | Key Outcome |
|---|---|
| Jaundiced gallbladder cancer cohort | 82 patients |
| Resection with negative margin | Only 4 patients |
| Matched nonjaundiced cohort | 158 patients |
| Median disease-specific survival in nonjaundiced cohort | 16 months |
| Median disease-specific survival in jaundiced cohort | 6 months |
| Disease-free survivors at 2 years in jaundiced cohort | None |

## Modern Management of Jaundiced Patients

- Jaundice warrants careful patient selection before radical surgery.
- Biliary decompression may be endoscopic or percutaneous.
- Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is often warranted after decompression.
- Treatment should further define tumor biology before resection.
- Adjusted analyses include N status, liver invasion, and resection margin.

## Minimally Invasive Techniques: Historical Concerns

| Concern | Reason |
|---|---|
| Intraperitoneal dissemination | Fear of cancer spread |
| Port site recurrence | Concern about seeding |
| Hepatic resection adequacy | Concern about insufficient parenchymal resection |
| Lymphadenectomy adequacy | Concern about incomplete nodal dissection |

## Current Minimally Invasive Evidence

- Minimally invasive techniques are increasingly used in other hepatic and pancreatobiliary malignancies.
- Use in gallbladder cancer resection has only recently gained recognition.
- Recent studies show extended cholecystectomy using minimally invasive techniques can achieve oncologic outcomes similar to open procedures.
- The principles of radical cholecystectomy, hepatic resection, and lymphadenectomy should remain the same as open surgery.

## Robotic-Assisted Radical Cholecystectomy Setup

| Setup Element | Description |
|---|---|
| Preferred approach | Robotic assisted |
| Patient position | Lithotomy |
| Assistant position | Standing between the patient's legs |
| Initial intraoperative step | Thorough liver ultrasonography |
| Sequence preference | Hepatoduodenal lymphadenectomy before hepatic resection |
| Rationale for sequence | Better visualization during liver resection |

## Surgical Algorithm by Stage

| Stage | Recommended Surgical Strategy |
|---|---|
| T1a | Simple cholecystectomy |
| T1b | Radical cholecystectomy with segment IVb and V hepatic resection and hepatoduodenal lymphadenectomy |
| T2 | Radical cholecystectomy with segment IVb and V hepatic resection and hepatoduodenal lymphadenectomy |
| T3 | Radical cholecystectomy with possible extensive hepatic resection, bile duct resection, or adjacent organ resection |
| T4 | Upfront extensive surgery generally unwarranted; consider neoadjuvant strategy and careful selection |

## Conclusion

- Current recommendations are stage-based.
- Simple cholecystectomy is appropriate for T1a disease.
- Radical cholecystectomy is appropriate for T1b to T2 disease.
- T3 disease may require radical cholecystectomy with adjacent organ resection.
- Overall prognosis remains poor, but staging, patient selection, and early recognition have improved.

## Take-Home Points

- Early recognition is essential for improving prognosis.
- Surgical resection at an early stage offers the best chance of long-term survival.
- Neoadjuvant therapy may help delineate tumor biology before radical resection.
- Open and minimally invasive techniques can achieve similar oncologic results when principles are maintained.
- Routine port site excision and routine bile duct resection are not advised.
- References are excluded per request.
